bracket: [Textbook misprint: two defects in the book's printed answer to this worked example. (i) The question labels its four items a, b, c, d while the answer list labels them i, ii, iii, iv — the two are in the same order, so i corresponds to a and so on. (ii) The reasoning for item iii reads "the fifth digit is greater than 5, so we **do** it and add 1 to the fourth digit"; the intended word is **drop**, as it is in items i, ii and iv. All four rounded values — 1.2, 12.6, 122.2 and 232 — are correct.]

[Textbook misprint: in Step III the book prints the divisor for carbon as 12.01 g, contradicting the atomic mass of 12.000 u its own stem supplies. The printed value 2.0225 is what 12.000 gives (24.27/12.000 = 2.0225); 12.01 would give 2.0208. So the divisor is the misprint and the value is right. The answer is unaffected either way — the H : C : Cl ratio is 2 : 1 : 1 and the molecular formula \(\mathrm{C_2H_4Cl_2}\) on both readings. The same 12.01 recurs in the empirical formula mass 49.48; with 12.000 it is 49.47, and the ratio 98.96/49.47 is still 2.]

[Textbook misprint: the book's printed final line reads "= 2.8 g of \(\mathrm{CaCO_3}\)", which contradicts its own question — the stem asks how much CaO is produced, and the line's own arithmetic (56/100 × 5 g) is the CaO fraction. As printed it asserts that decomposing 5 g of calcium carbonate yields 2.8 g of calcium carbonate. The species has been corrected to CaO above; the value 2.8 g is the book's and is correct.]

[Textbook note (not an error): the book sets the part labels (a) and (b) inline in the middle of a sentence, so the line prints as "...because it produces (a) smaller amount of \((\mathrm{NH_2})_2\mathrm{CO}\)) (b) The molar mass..." — the (a) stands where the article "a" belongs, there is an unmatched closing bracket, and part (b) starts mid-sentence. The layout has been restored above so the three parts read as parts; every number, quantity and conclusion is the book's own and is unchanged.]

[Textbook note (not an error): the item labels in this block run A to J at the foot of one page and then resume at **M** at the head of the next — the book prints no items K or L in "Answer the following questions". Verified on both printed pages. The block therefore holds eleven questions with thirteen labels; the printed label M is preserved here rather than renumbered.]

[Textbook note (not an error): the atomic-mass list printed with this item gives Pb, P, O, K, Cr, Na and N but omits **H**, which part (c) needs — macrocosmic salt \(\mathrm{NaNH_4HPO_4 \cdot 4H_2O}\) contains thirteen hydrogen atoms per formula unit. H = 1 is supplied by the list printed with the item immediately above and is used in the answer.]

[Textbook answer-key error: the printed answer is \(\mathrm{FeSO_4}\), which omits the water of crystallisation. The question describes a **hydrated** salt and supplies 0.4532 g of water explicitly, and that mass fixes the hydration exactly: 0.4532/18 = 0.02518 mol of water against 0.2014/56 = 0.003596 mol of iron, a ratio of 7.00. The complete empirical formula of the substance described is \(\mathrm{FeSO_4 \cdot 7H_2O}\). The printed \(\mathrm{FeSO_4}\) is correct for the anhydrous part alone — its own O count is 4.00 — but it does not answer the question as asked.]

[Textbook misprint: parts (a) and (b) are printed as "(3.26 104) (1.54 106)" and "(8.39 107) (4.53 109)" — in both, the multiplication sign is missing AND the powers of ten are set on the baseline instead of raised. Verified on the page at 5x magnification; parts (c) and (d) of the same item set their exponents correctly, which is what identifies (a) and (b) as the defect. They are solved above in their intended reading, \((3.26 \times 10^4)(1.54 \times 10^6)\) and \((8.39 \times 10^7)(4.53 \times 10^9)\).]

[Textbook misprint: in part (c) the second term is printed as "8.1 \(10^{-4}\)" with the multiplication sign dropped. Verified on the page at 5x magnification; parts (a), (b) and (d) on the same lines set theirs correctly. It is solved above as \(8.1 \times 10^{-4}\).]

[Textbook answer-key error: the printed answer is "±0.07736% 0.1027%". The second figure is correct — the relative error is \((0.7783 - 0.7791)/0.7791 \times 100 = -0.1027\%\), to the digit. The first is not. This chapter defines relative deviation as **mean absolute deviation ÷ mean**, and applies that definition in its own Problem 2.6; here the three masses are 0.7783, 0.7780 and 0.7786 g, the mean is 0.7783 g, the absolute deviations are 0.0000, 0.0003 and 0.0003 g, and the mean absolute deviation is therefore ±0.0002 g — giving a relative deviation of 0.0002/0.7783 × 100 = **0.026 %**, not 0.077 %. Eight candidate routes to the printed 0.07736 % were tested and none reproduces it; the closest is 0.0771 %, obtained by dividing the SUM of the three deviations by the mean instead of their mean, which is itself a departure from the chapter's own definition. So the printed figure cannot be reconstructed exactly, and it is roughly three times the correct relative deviation.]
